1	# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do
2	
3	The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
4	long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. It is
5	off since 2026-10-13 ([Turned off](#turned-off)), and the instruction is kept here ([The
6	instruction, as it was](#the-instruction-as-it-was)). This file also holds what was found out
7	about the lock on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's place, and what
8	happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's own tests, of
9	2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.
10	
11	The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, no hook is built, and the
12	instruction, kept on 2026-10-12, was taken out of `custom.md` the day after.
13	
14	## What the lock is when it is on
15	
16	- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
17	  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
18	  touches the lock.
19	- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
20	  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
21	- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
22	  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
23	  the instruction has it stop then.
24	- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.
25	
26	## What a hook could do
27	
28	A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
29	reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
30	`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script
31	hooked to a session's start, to each prompt, and to its end, logging what it was given and
32	leaving a watcher process behind. Wink ran it in four sessions under Claude Code 2.1.296: one
33	exited, one killed with `kill -9`, one whose terminal was closed, one resumed.
34	
35	- From the documents:
36	  - A session-start hook fires on a fresh start, a resume, a `/clear`, a compaction, and a fork.
37	  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
38	  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
39	    every call.
40	  - A session-end hook has a second and a half and cannot refuse.
41	  - A hook runs in a process session of its own, with no controlling terminal.
42	- From the probe:
43	  - A process a hook leaves behind outlives the hook, and Claude Code does not end it.
44	  - A hook is given `CLAUDE_PID`, the Claude Code process, which is also the hook's parent. The
45	    documents do not name that variable.
46	  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
47	  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
48	  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
49	    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
50	    as a lock should is the process id.
51	- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
52	  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
53	  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
54	- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
55	  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.
56	
57	## What two sessions do with no lock
58	
59	Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
60	with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
61	the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
62	operation log.
63	
64	- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
65	  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
66	  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
67	    commit under B's title.
68	  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
69	- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
70	  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
71	    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
72	  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
73	    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
74	  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
75	    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
76	    deleted them.
77	  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
78	    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
79	- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
80	  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
81	    same second, and every line of it parses.
82	  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
83	    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
84	- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
85	  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
86	    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
87	- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
88	  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
89	  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

# The session lock, and what two sessions in one workspace do

The session lock is the exclusive `flock` on `.agent-running` that an agent session holds for as
long as it runs, taken because an instruction in `custom.md` tells the agent to take it. It is
off since 2026-10-13 ([Turned off](#turned-off)), and the instruction is kept here ([The
instruction, as it was](#the-instruction-as-it-was)). This file also holds what was found out
about the lock on 2026-10-12: what Claude Code's hooks could do in the agent's place, and what
happens when two sessions work in one workspace with no lock at all. The lock's own tests, of
2026-10-11, are in the landmark `docs: the session lock is settled as flock`.

The short of it: two sessions lose no data and leave a wrong record, no hook is built, and the
instruction, kept on 2026-10-12, was taken out of `custom.md` the day after.

## What the lock is when it is on

- The agent takes it by hand: `flock -xn .agent-running true` as a probe, then
  `flock -xn .agent-running sleep infinity` as a background command. `vc-x1` has no code that
  touches the lock.
- Nothing releases it. The kernel drops a `flock` when the process holding it exits, and Claude
  Code ends a session's background commands when the session ends.
- It closes no race and needs none closed: a `flock` has one winner whoever asks. A session that
  loses between its probe and its holder learns of it seconds later, when the holder exits, and
  the instruction has it stop then.
- Its weakness is that an agent has to read the instruction and follow it.

## What a hook could do

A hook is a command Claude Code itself runs at a moment in a session, whether or not the agent
reads anything. The documents were read 2026-10-12 (the hooks reference and guide at
`code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks`), and what they do not say was found with a probe: a script

  - It cannot refuse a session. It can add to the agent's context or show a message.
  - A prompt hook can stop a prompt before the agent sees it, and a hook on tool calls can deny
    every call.

    documents do not name that variable.
  - The watcher saw the Claude Code process gone within a second or two of each ending.
  - The session-end hook fired on the `/exit` and on the closed terminal, and not on the kill.
  - A `/clear` ends the session and starts another, under a new session id, in the same
    process. A resume keeps the session id in a new process. So the one thing that lasts as long
    as a lock should is the process id.
- The design that follows: a script at a session's start takes the `flock`, writes the process
  id into `.agent-running`, and leaves a holder that exits when that process is gone, and the
  same script at each prompt stops a prompt from a process that is not the owner.
- It was not built, wink's call. It rests on a variable the documents do not name and on hook
  behaviour they do not state, and what it guards against turned out to lose no data.

## What two sessions do with no lock

Three tests, run by wink in a scratch workspace made by `vc-x1 init xxx --repo local=<parent>`,
with two Claude Code sessions, A and B, open in it at once and no agent-files to tell either of
the other. Each result was read from the two repos, their remotes, the transcripts, and jj's
operation log.

- Pushes minutes apart. A wrote `a.txt`, B wrote `b.txt`, A pushed, then B pushed.
  - A's work commit held both files, B's under A's title.
  - B's push found nothing left to commit in the work-repo, said so, and made an agent-repo
    commit under B's title.
  - Two agent-repo commits then named the one work commit, which named A's alone.
- Pushes in the same second, each session's command sleeping to the top of the minute.
  - B's push committed both sessions' edits, pushed the work-repo, and died with
    `error: Concurrent checkout`, its agent-repo stage not run.
  - A's push reported success. Its work commit held none of A's edit, and it made no agent-repo
    commit, taking B's as its partner, so two work commits named one agent-repo commit.
  - B's commit also held 23 empty files, `.bashrc`, `.gitconfig`, `.claude/settings.json`, and
    the rest: the names the agent sandbox puts on disk while a command of A's ran. A's commit
    deleted them.
  - jj recorded "reconcile divergent operations" twice, with no conflict and no divergent
    change. Both remotes ended with everything and the tree was right.
- One session resumed in two terminals, `claude --resume <id>` in each.
  - Both wrote to the one transcript file, eight prompts and replies, two of the prompts in the
    same second, and every line of it parses.
  - The conversation forked without a word: each terminal's messages follow its own, so the
    file holds two branches, interleaved line by line.
- In all three every transcript line parses and nothing either session wrote was lost.
  - A session writes a transcript file named by its session id, so two sessions write two
    files, and a file two processes share is appended to a whole line at a time.
- What goes wrong is the record: a title that does not say what its commit holds, a trailer that
  names the wrong session or one of two, a push that dies with an error that explains nothing,
  and a transcript that reads as two conversations shuffled.

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) Two `vc-x1` runs in one workspace can overlap, a user's two terminals
included, and nothing serializes them. A lock for it was considered and is not added, wink's call,
2026-10-13: what it costs is more than what it prevents here, the reason the session lock was
turned off ([session-lock.md](session-lock.md#turned-off)). The design is kept for the day the
overlap is met in real use.

  purpose, two pushes started in the same second in the tests of 2026-10-12. One died with
  `error: Concurrent checkout` partway, and the other took the first's agent-repo commit as its
  partner, so two work commits name one ([session-lock.md](session-lock.md#what-two-sessions-do-with-no-lock)).
- What jj covers: two jj commands run at once do not corrupt a repo. We think each records an
  operation and the next command merges the two, from what we know of jj and not from a test.
- What jj does not cover: a sequence. A `vc-x1 push` is a commit in each repo, the trailers that
  pair them, and two pushes to the remotes, and jj serializes each of those and not the run.
- The overlap that is left: a user's run started beside the agent's, two of the user's own, or two
  sessions' runs, the session lock being off. [At
  rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push) has the agent stop before the user
  squash-pushes, which keeps the first of them rare.
- The lock is `.vc-x1-running` at the workspace root, wink's thought: `vc-x1` takes it itself,
  exclusive and without waiting, for as long as one run lasts, so two runs in one workspace
  cannot overlap, whoever started them.
  - The process that asks is the process that holds, so a session's own `vc-x1` commands never
    collide with one another.
  - It was to be how rename and delete check for a running agent. They now ask for no lock ([What
    stops delete and rename](../TODO.md#what-stops-delete-and-rename)).
- It guards a run and nothing between runs. Two agents editing one working copy share one `@`,
  and a push takes the working copy whole, so one agent's edits land in the other's commit
  even when they touch different files. No lock guards that, the session lock being off.
- The commands that write take it, `push`, `squash-push`, and `sync`, narrowed 2026-10-12. Every
  invocation taking it was wink's call of 2026-10-11, the simplest rule.
- To settle in its cycle: a run with no workspace yet (`init`, `clone`, `--help`) has no root to
  lock, and a `vc-x1` that starts another `vc-x1` in the same workspace would refuse itself.

### vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for a run that writes

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) Two `vc-x1` runs in one workspace can overlap, a user's two terminals
included, and nothing serializes them. A lock for it was considered and is not added, wink's call,
2026-10-13: what it costs is more than what it prevents here, the reason the session lock was
turned off ([session-lock.md](session-lock.md#turned-off)). The design is kept for the day the
overlap is met in real use.

- What would reopen it: two runs overlapping outside a test. The one overlap seen was made on
  purpose, two pushes started in the same second in the tests of 2026-10-12. One died with
  `error: Concurrent checkout` partway, and the other took the first's agent-repo commit as its
  partner, so two work commits name one ([session-lock.md](session-lock.md#what-two-sessions-do-with-no-lock)).
- What jj covers: two jj commands run at once do not corrupt a repo. We think each records an
  operation and the next command merges the two, from what we know of jj and not from a test.
- What jj does not cover: a sequence. A `vc-x1 push` is a commit in each repo, the trailers that
  pair them, and two pushes to the remotes, and jj serializes each of those and not the run.
- The overlap that is left: a user's run started beside the agent's, two of the user's own, or two
  sessions' runs, the session lock being off. [At
  rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push) has the agent stop before the user
  squash-pushes, which keeps the first of them rare.
- The lock is `.vc-x1-running` at the workspace root, wink's thought: `vc-x1` takes it itself,
  exclusive and without waiting, for as long as one run lasts, so two runs in one workspace
  cannot overlap, whoever started them.
  - The process that asks is the process that holds, so a session's own `vc-x1` commands never
    collide with one another.
  - It was to be how rename and delete check for a running agent. They now ask for no lock ([What
    stops delete and rename](../TODO.md#what-stops-delete-and-rename)).
- It guards a run and nothing between runs. Two agents editing one working copy share one `@`,
  and a push takes the working copy whole, so one agent's edits land in the other's commit
  even when they touch different files. No lock guards that, the session lock being off.
- The commands that write take it, `push`, `squash-push`, and `sync`, narrowed 2026-10-12. Every
  invocation taking it was wink's call of 2026-10-11, the simplest rule.
- To settle in its cycle: a run with no workspace yet (`init`, `clone`, `--help`) has no root to
  lock, and a `vc-x1` that starts another `vc-x1` in the same workspace would refuse itself.

### docs: vc-x1 takes no lock for a run

(wink + agent, 2026-10-13) Two `vc-x1` runs in one workspace can overlap, and a Todo entry planned
a lock, `.vc-x1-running`, that `vc-x1` would take for every run. Every run would pay for it, and
what it prevents does not come up with one user running one session at a time. The Todo entry
picked is "vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every run". The entry "The parked planning of
2026-10-12 is run as a cycle" is ended by this cycle too.

#### Deliberation

- The lock is not added, wink's call.
  - Its cost is more than its worth, the reason the session lock was turned off.
  - The one overlap seen was made on purpose, two pushes started in the same second in the tests
    of 2026-10-12, and it lost no data.
- The entry moves to the backlog and is not deleted, wink's call, so the design is not lost.
  - Its text is the parked commit's, where the entry had already been moved to the backlog,
    brought up to date: the decision, what would reopen it, and the session lock being off.
  - The continuation notes had it written fresh and the parked text not taken. Wink reversed
    that at the opening.
- The bookmark `parked-planning-change-20261012` is deleted at Land, locally and on `origin`,
  wink's call. The backlog entry is what was wanted from it.
  - Dropped with it, drafts that were no cycle's rung:
    - `symlink` taking `create` or `remove`, and no `vc-x1 delete`
    - the Ideas entry for a shared work-repo's config, with `clone` taking the agent-repo's
      directory
    - an ochid carrying no path
    - the config's version field.
  - Its commit is `85f87d76`, change `wkytxkqo`, findable by that id in a clone that fetched it
    and nowhere on the remote once the bookmark is gone.
- Two lines of the entry "Improve init and add rename and delete subcommands" leaned on a lock
  and are brought up to date, the agent's placing: what stops delete and rename asks for no
  lock, and the lock's experiment with fresh sessions is gone.
- The third acceptance check of **docs: turn off the session lock** is recorded here, as that
  cycle's record said it would be.
- A single-step cycle, with a bare version and no `-dev` name, the cycle being documents alone.

#### Solution

The lock `vc-x1` was to take for a run is recorded as considered and not added, and the planning
parked on 2026-10-12 is ended.

- The backlog holds the entry, [vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for a run that
  writes](notes/todo-backlog.md#vc-x1-takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-a-run-that-writes), with the
  decision and what would reopen it.
- The two Todo entries are removed, and [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md#what-was-decided)
  points at the backlog entry.

#### Acceptance check

- `vc-x1 validate` passes.
- `rg 'vc-x1-running|takes-a-lock-of-its-own-for-every-run|parked-planning' TODO.md notes/`
  finds `.vc-x1-running` in the backlog entry and nothing else.
- The session lock is off, the check **docs: turn off the session lock** left as not run. Passed:
  the session that ran this cycle started after that Land, acquainted without running `flock`,
  and did not say "Lock taken." The probe from another terminal was not run, wink having removed
  `.agent-running`, so there is no file to hold a lock on.

#### Ladder

- docs: vc-x1 takes no lock for a run (current)

136	### Commit-body form
137	
138	The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139	shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142	statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143	
144	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145	  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146	  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147	  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148	  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150	  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151	  to be more than one commit.
152	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153	  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154	  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
155	- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
156	  form, the general form at its smallest.
157	- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
158	  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
159	  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
160	
161	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
162	pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
163	typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
164	read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
165	flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
166	a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.
167

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with

    it a string and never touches the filesystem.

  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

236	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / commit)
237	
238	([why](rationale.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit))
239	
240	A ladder step and its commit description share a *title* shape, a [Conventional
241	Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`, an optional
242	`(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in
243	the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the [Commit-body
244	form](#commit-body-form), the ladder's are conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
245	above). The shared template:
246	
247	```
248	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
249	<optional prose intro>
250	  - <optional item>
251	    <optional prose intro>
252	      - <optional sub-item>
253	      ...
254	```
255	
256	The two surfaces apply it as:
257	
258	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title
259	  reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the
260	  closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker. Its position in the
261	  list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its text says so. Detail
262	  lives not on the rung but in its subsection under the ladder, headed by the rung's exact
263	  title (see the protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
264	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose (see
265	  [Commit description](../AGENTS.md#commit-description)).
266	
267	The title is **identical** across both for a given step, so a step's ladder entry and its commit
268	title line up verbatim. The rung's subsection heading carries the same title, a third
269	surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
270	protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
271	
272	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct descriptive
273	title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The block's title heading carries
274	the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the bookends below). To keep a
275	cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem
276	(e.g. `config loader`).
277	
278	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a suffix, "
279	opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
280	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
281	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the block's title heading carries
282	it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the closing rung's subsection anchor
283	clear of the title heading's. A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare
284	title, in both repos and in its one ladder rung ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The type
285	repeats across the pair even though the bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make
286	them scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.
287	
288	### Commit titles and descriptions
289	
290	([why](rationale.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions))
291	
292	The vocabulary over the structure: [Conventional-commit
293	shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) holds what a title and body are shaped like, and
294	this section holds what may fill them. The title is a [Conventional
295	Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), `<type>: <short description>` with an optional
296	`(scope)`, at the width in [Line widths](#line-widths). The body is the [Commit-body
297	form](#commit-body-form), wrapped per Line widths, with no version in title or body, no file list,
298	and no deliberation. `vc-x1 push` gives both repos' commits the same title and body. `ochid:` is

form](#commit-body-form), the ladder's are conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
above). The shared template:

```
<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`

  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...

surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
